prompt: What is your main job as a referee?
options: Protect the fairness of the challenge for every athlete
Help athletes finish as quickly as possible
Make sure the strongest athletes win
Keep spectators entertained
feedback: Spartan challenges every athlete. You protect the integrity of the race, treat everyone equally and keep it fair.

prompt: A team-mate of yours is clearly exhausted at your obstacle. Which part of the referee code applies?
options: Safety first: let them skip it
Be impartial: judge the action, never the athlete
Escalate doubt: let them pass and tell the Head Referee later
Follow the rules only for athletes you do not know
feedback: You judge the action against the rule, whoever the athlete is.

prompt: You spot a loose fixing on your obstacle just before the first athlete arrives. What does the code say?
options: Wait and see if it holds
Tell the athletes to take care
Spot the danger and report it at once
Note it for your end-of-day report
feedback: Safety first means spotting danger and reporting it at once.

prompt: Two athletes make the same mistake at your obstacle, an hour apart. How should you treat them?
options: Be easier on the second, as you are tired
Be stricter on the second, as the first was a warning
Decide by how hard each one tried
Apply the same standard to both
feedback: The code says to follow the rules with the same standard every time.

prompt: You are not sure how a rule applies to what you have just seen. What does the code tell you to do?
options: Take it to the Head Referee
Give the athlete the benefit of the doubt
Choose the stricter option to be safe
Ask the other athletes nearby
feedback: Doubt is escalated to the Head Referee, not settled by guesswork.

prompt: Which athletes make up the Competitive category?
options: Age Group and Open
Elite and Age Group
Elite and Open
Open only
feedback: Competitive is the Elite and Age Group racers. Open is the other category.

prompt: The event runs Open athletes differently from Competitive athletes at your obstacle. What do you do?
options: Use the Competitive way for everyone
Use whichever you think is fairer
Follow the event's instructions for the category in front of you
Ask the athlete which way they prefer
feedback: The two categories can be run differently, so always follow the event's instructions for each.

prompt: Which of these is one of the four parts of the referee code?
options: Be quick
Be friendly
Be lenient
Be impartial
feedback: The code is: be impartial, safety first, follow the rules, and escalate doubt.

prompt: Which race-day step comes straight after check-in?
options: Inspection
Briefing
Officiating
Handover
feedback: The order is briefing, check-in, inspection, officiating, handover and report.

prompt: What do you collect when you check in and confirm your assignment?
options: Your athlete list
Your kit and the rules
A penalty tally sheet
Your obstacle's finish times
feedback: After checking in you collect your kit and the rules.

prompt: The event has a radio or chat group for referees. What should you do?
options: Ignore it unless you need help
Leave it to the Head Referee
Join it, and report to the Head Referee
Join it only after the first athlete passes
feedback: Being race-ready includes joining the event's radio or chat if there is one, and reporting to the Head Referee.

prompt: What do you check when you inspect your obstacle before the race?
options: The athletes' headband numbers
The finish line timing
The spectators' viewing area
The setup and any hazards
feedback: You inspect for safety: the setup and any hazards.

prompt: You walk your obstacle's route before the race. What should the walk include?
options: How athletes will flow, and the penalty loop
Only the obstacle itself
Only the start of the course
The route to the finish area
feedback: Walk the route: how athletes flow, and the penalty loop.

prompt: You have checked your obstacle's rule and walked the route. What is the last part of getting ready?
options: Practise the obstacle yourself
Choose where you will stand, and brief any marshals
Take the athletes' headband numbers early
Ask the Head Referee to stand with you
feedback: You choose your view, and brief any marshals, before the first athlete arrives.

prompt: In the escalation chain, what is the referee's part?
options: Review, direct and interpret
Take further action on timing
Observe, apply the rule and record
Decide the overall results
feedback: The referee observes, applies the rule and records. Reviewing and interpreting is the Head Referee's part.

prompt: Who takes further action where it is needed, after the Head Referee has reviewed a case?
options: The nearest marshal
The other referees on the course
The athlete's team captain
The Race Director or the timing team
feedback: The Race Director or the timing team take further action where needed.

prompt: Before you make a call, what should you recognise first about the obstacle?
options: Which of the three types it is
How many athletes are waiting
How tired the athlete looks
How long it takes to complete
feedback: Mandatory, multiple attempt and single attempt each follow a different rule path.

prompt: An athlete fails the Hercules Hoist, then gives up. What applies at a multiple attempt obstacle?
options: They are disqualified
They take the penalty
They must keep trying
They finish the race without a penalty
feedback: At a multiple attempt obstacle the athlete may keep trying, or give up and take the penalty.

prompt: At a single attempt obstacle, an athlete has not yet reached the point where the attempt starts. May they reset?
options: No, they are already committed
Only if the Head Referee agrees
Yes, before that point they may still reset
Yes, but they must take the penalty
feedback: Each obstacle's rule says when the attempt starts. Before that point the athlete may still reset.

prompt: Which of these is a single attempt obstacle?
options: The Rope Climb
The Hercules Hoist
The barbed wire crawl
The Z Wall
feedback: The Monkey Bars, the Multi-Rig and the Z Wall are single attempt. The Rope Climb and Hercules Hoist are multiple attempt, and the barbed wire crawl is mandatory.

prompt: An athlete runs round the fire jump instead of jumping it. What normally follows?
options: Disqualification, unless the Race Director gives a time penalty
A penalty loop
30 burpees
Nothing, if they rejoin the course
feedback: The fire jump is mandatory. Failing it normally means disqualification, though the Race Director may give a time penalty instead.

prompt: At the Spear Throw, how far must the athlete move away before the throw counts?
options: 1 metre
2 metres
5 metres
Out of the lane
feedback: One of the four things to watch is that the athlete moves 2 metres away before it counts.

prompt: An athlete at the Spear Throw hits the target in the next lane. What is wrong?
options: Both feet must be behind the barrier
The spear must stay in the target
The throw must be at the target in their own lane
The athlete must move 2 metres away
feedback: The throw must be at the target in the same lane.

prompt: A spear sticks in the target, then slides out and its tail touches the ground. Does it count?
options: Yes, it stuck first
Yes, if the athlete moved 2 metres away
Only if it was a close throw
No: it must stay in the target without touching the ground
feedback: The spear must stick and stay there. Once it has stopped, no part of it may touch the ground.

prompt: An athlete does half of the designated penalty loop and carries on. Is that enough?
options: No: the penalty is the whole of the loop
Yes, if the loop was busy
Yes, if they were close to passing
Only for Open athletes
feedback: The penalty has to be the one the event sets: the whole of the designated loop, or the burpees where the event says so.

prompt: An athlete argues with you, so you want to add burpees. What does the penalty rule say?
options: Add 10 burpees for rudeness
Never give a penalty of your own
Add the burpees but tell the Head Referee
Add a lap of the penalty loop
feedback: You give the event's penalty and never one of your own.

prompt: Where the event says burpees are the penalty, how many do athletes do at a Stadion event?
feedback: The penalty is 30 burpees, or 15 at Stadion events.

prompt: Where might an athlete's skipped penalty loop be found?
options: Only at the finish line
Only if the athlete admits it
Only by the timing team
On course, or in the review before the awards
feedback: It can be found on course or in the review before the awards, and 10 minutes are added.

prompt: An athlete jumps at the top of a burpee but keeps their hands down by their hips. What is missing?
options: Hands above the ears
Chest to the ground
Hips and knees fully extended
A clap at the bottom
feedback: A burpee needs chest down, hips and knees fully extended, and a jump with the hands above the ears.

prompt: An athlete is unsure whether a burpee was good and asks you for a count. What is right?
options: You call the count for them
They count their own, and may repeat one they are unsure of
You tell them to carry on
You coach them on the standard as they go
feedback: The athlete counts their own burpees. You watch the standard and help video review, and don't coach.

prompt: After review, an athlete at a standard OCR race missed 4 burpees. What is added?
options: 4 minutes
10 minutes
2 minutes
30 seconds
feedback: Each of the first 10 missed burpees adds 30 seconds, so 4 missed adds 2 minutes.

prompt: After review, an athlete at a Stadion event missed 7 burpees. What is added?
options: 3 minutes 30 seconds
10 minutes
2 minutes 30 seconds
5 minutes in total
feedback: At Stadion events, missing more than 5 adds 5 minutes in total.

prompt: An athlete challenges your call and starts to argue. What should you do?
options: Stay calm and refer the challenge to the Head Referee
Argue your case until they accept it
Change the call to end the dispute
Ignore them and move on
feedback: Explain the rule briefly and respectfully, don't argue, and refer a challenge to the Head Referee.

prompt: An athlete asks why you made a call. How should you explain it?
options: In as much detail as possible
Briefly, respectfully and accurately
By telling them to ask someone else
By comparing them with other athletes
feedback: Professional conversations stop disputes growing.

prompt: Which detail belongs in your report to the Head Referee?
options: Your opinion of the athlete's attitude
How the athlete compares with others
The headband number
Your guess at why it happened
feedback: Report the headband number, the obstacle and where it is, what you saw, when it happened, and who you told.

prompt: An athlete is struggling on the Monkey Bars. You know a tip that would help. What do you do?
options: Call the tip out quietly
Give the tip, then log it
Give the tip only if they ask
Say nothing, as you must never coach during an attempt
feedback: Never coach an athlete during an attempt. Watch the action and protect safety.

prompt: An athlete at your obstacle is from your own club. What does your position of trust ask of you?
options: Avoid any bias and watch the action
Give them a little extra help
Check them more strictly to look fair
Pass every call on them to the Head Referee
feedback: Your position is one of trust: watch the action, avoid any bias, and protect safety.

prompt: When you choose your view of an obstacle, what should you know about the approach?
options: How quickly athletes will finish
Where athletes enter, and where the lane boundaries are
Who is likely to fail
Which athletes are Elite
feedback: A good call starts with a clear view: know the entry and the lane boundaries.

prompt: At an obstacle with a bell, what must your view let you see at the finish?
options: The athlete's face
The next athlete in the queue
The success condition, such as the bell
The penalty loop
feedback: At the finish you must see the success condition, such as the bell.

prompt: Which of these is one of the five rules for race day?
options: Speed first
Athletes decide close calls
Keep your view loose
Consistency always
feedback: The five rules are: safety first, consistency always, know the obstacle, give the correct penalty, and escalate uncertainty.
